name: gemmi
why: Macromolecular crystallography tools let you read real protein structure files, a close call on whether utilities go far enough.

brief.what_it_is: GEMMI is a C++ library for macromolecular crystallography, shipped with a command-line program also named gemmi that bundles many small subcommands. It reads and writes coordinate files (PDB, mmCIF, mmJSON), CIF/STAR files, reflection data (MTZ and SF-mmCIF, plus XDS_ASCII), CCP4/MRC density maps, and restraint or monomer-library CIF files. Output is usually a converted or modified file, a text report, or a histogram in the terminal. The project also has Python bindings, partial WebAssembly bindings, and an online viewer and stats pages.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says GEMMI can help if you work with macromolecular models, refinement restraints, crystallographic reflections, density maps, crystallographic symmetries, or just CIF/STAR files, where the C in CIF stands for Crystallographic. It is an open-source project of CCP4 and Global Phasing Ltd, which the README describes as two major providers of software for macromolecular crystallography.
brief.how_it_works: The command-line program is a set of small subcommands (for example validate, grep, convert, set, mtz, map, sfcalc), each run as gemmi followed by the subcommand name. The grep subcommand parses CIF syntax rather than doing plain text matching, so it prints values from both name-value pairs and loops. The docs say the whole compressed PDB mmCIF archive can be searched in roughly 10 to 30 minutes on an average computer, and that output pipes into standard Unix tools such as sort, awk, and uniq.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, I found nothing in the README about required accounts, runtimes, or first-run configuration. The README says the C++ library is currently C++14, and the Python bindings and Fortran 2003+ interface (still in progress) are separate pieces. The installation page of the docs (gemmi.readthedocs.io, Installation section) exists but I did not fetch it, so build and dependency details are unverified. The program docs mention $CLIBD_MON and $PDB_DIR environment variables for some features.
brief.standout: It treats CIF syntax as the core, so the command-line tools work on real archive-scale data (the whole PDB mmCIF archive) and the grep subcommand avoids the failures of plain Unix grep on looped tags. It pairs a C++ library with a CLI, Python bindings, and browser builds, and its subcommands reach from file conversion to crystallographic calculations such as sfcalc, sf2map, and mask.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as I can tell. The docs are at version 0.7.6-dev, the README carries a CI badge and a copyright line running through 2025, and the project has a JOSS paper. I did not check a last-commit date or latest release date, so this rests on those signals rather than dated evidence.
brief.caveats: The homepage URL only returned a redirect page with no content, so I took the project description from the GitHub README and docs instead. The README gives no install commands. The docs page I read was cut off at 40000 characters, so I did not see the full subcommand list or per-command details past the cif2mtz section. The docs call one command gemmi diff while the usage text lists cifdiff, so exact names may need checking against gemmi -h. The license is MPLv2, or at your option LGPLv3. The scout note's 'close call on whether utilities go far enough' is not something I could judge from these pages; the subcommand list is broad.
quotes: The library comes with a command-line program which is also named gemmi; running a program is easier than calling a library function.

judge.reason: GEMMI turns specialized crystallographic formats and calculations into a usable toolkit, and its syntax-aware grep can explore archive-scale CIF data correctly.

entry.title: gemmi
entry.tldr: A command-line toolkit for reading, searching and converting protein structure files, with a CIF-aware grep that can sweep the whole Protein Data Bank archive.
entry.deeper_look:
GEMMI is a C++ library for macromolecular crystallography, and it ships with a command-line program, also called gemmi, that bundles many small subcommands. It reads and writes coordinate files (PDB, mmCIF, mmJSON), CIF/STAR files, reflection data (MTZ, SF-mmCIF, XDS_ASCII), CCP4/MRC density maps, and restraint CIF files. Output is usually a converted file, a text report, or a histogram in the terminal.

The subcommand that makes the best first stop is grep. CIF is the format behind the Protein Data Bank's structure files, and its data lives in both name-value pairs and loops, which plain Unix grep handles badly. In the docs' words, "Gemmi-grep parses the CIF syntax and prints values from both name-value pairs and loops." The output pipes into sort, awk and uniq, so a question like "which experimental methods appear across the archive" becomes a one-line shell pipeline.

The docs claim that searching the whole compressed mmCIF archive from the PDB (35GB of gzipped files) takes between 10 and 30 minutes on an average computer. That is the door into the larger idea: the structures of proteins and other biomolecules are public, stored as plain text, and you can interrogate them like any other dataset. Other subcommands go further into crystallography proper, such as map, mask and sfcalc, for density maps, bulk-solvent masks and structure factors.

GEMMI is an open-source project of CCP4 and Global Phasing Ltd, two major providers of crystallography software. It also has Python bindings, partial WebAssembly bindings, and an online viewer, so the same code can be reached from a script or a browser.
entry.install:
brew install gemmi
# Some features read $CLIBD_MON and $PDB_DIR; set them only if you use those. You need a CIF or mmCIF file to try most commands, for example one downloaded from the Protein Data Bank.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the top-level usage and the list of subcommands, such as align, blobs, cif2json, convert, grep and validate.
Prints one tag's value from a structure file, as a line with the block name and value, e.g. 5FYI:0.2358.
Shows usage for the map subcommand, which summarizes a CCP4 density map, plots a histogram, and can write masks or re-gridded maps.

entry.whats_unique: It treats CIF syntax as the core, so its tools work on archive-scale data where plain grep fails on looped tags. One project covers a C++ library, a CLI, Python bindings and browser builds.
entry.caveats: The brief could not confirm a last-commit date, though the docs are at 0.7.6-dev and the README's copyright runs through 2025; the docs call one command gemmi diff while the usage text lists cifdiff, so check gemmi -h for exact names.
